title: Back-rank weakness
author: Agent Chess
intro: White to move and mate in 2. Black's king is boxed in by its own pawns. Find the way in.

hints: The only black piece guarding the back rank is the rook on a8.
What happens if that rook is forced to leave the a8 square?
Your queen and rook are lined up on the c-file. Use the front one as bait.
line.explain: A queen sacrifice! The check forces Black's rook to take, and that pulls it onto c8, right in front of your rook.

Qxg7+.text: The king simply takes the queen and the attack is over.

wrong.Qc7: Quiet moves give Black time to play ...h6 and make an escape square.

Rc2.text: White is still winning, but Black now plays ...h6 or ...g6 and the back-rank mate is gone. There's a mate in 2 right now.

wrong.*: Black's king has no escape squares. Look for a check on the 8th rank that Black can only answer one way.

line.explain: Forced: the king can't move (f8 and h8 are covered along the rank, and its own pawns block the rest).

hints: The c-file is open all the way now.
line.explain: Checkmate. The rook takes on c8 and the king is trapped behind its own pawns.

conclusion: This is the classic back-rank mate. When a king has no escape square (here f7, g7 and h7 are all its own pawns), a single heavy piece on the 8th rank can mate. The queen sacrifice works because it deflects the only defender, the a8 rook, onto a square where your rook can take it with mate. In your own games, a quiet ...h6 (or h3 for White) early on removes this whole danger.
